paragraphs.heading: The first stage
paragraphs.text: An embryo is the first stage of development in a multicellular organism. In species that reproduce sexually, it begins just after a male sperm cell fertilizes a female egg cell. A developing human is usually called an embryo until the ninth week after conception, and a fetus after that. For other organisms, the word can cover any early stage before birth or hatching.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word first appeared in English in the mid-14th century as embryon. It came through Medieval Latin from the Greek émbryon, meaning young one, which is built from parts meaning in and to swell, to be full.

paragraphs.heading: The first divisions
paragraphs.text: The egg and sperm fuse into a single-celled zygote, which then divides many times. This rapid run of divisions, called cleavage, does not make the embryo bigger; the cells get smaller as their number grows. The cells, called blastomeres, form a solid ball, and at a certain size, the morula stage, the ball takes in fluid and opens a cavity called the blastocoel. It is then called a blastula, or in mammals a blastocyst, and a mammalian blastocyst hatches before implanting in the lining of the womb.

paragraphs.heading: Three germ layers
paragraphs.text: Gastrulation comes next, as the embryo forms two or more layers of cells, called germ layers. Animals that make two layers, Cnidaria for example, are diploblastic, while those that make three, from flatworms to humans, are triploblastic. The three layers are the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, and every tissue and organ of the adult can be traced to one of them. The ectoderm makes the skin's outer layer and the nervous system; the mesoderm makes the vascular system, muscle, bone and connective tissue; the endoderm makes the digestive organs and the linings of the digestive and respiratory systems.

paragraphs.heading: Building organs
paragraphs.text: As germ layer cells move during gastrulation, the round embryo folds inward into a cup-like shape. Neurulation then forms the nervous system, and organogenesis, as its name suggests, is when organs form. In organogenesis, interactions between molecules and cells prompt groups of cells from the germ layers to become cell types for specific organs. For example, some ectoderm cells separate from the rest and specialize into the brain, spinal cord or peripheral nerves.

paragraphs.heading: When an embryo stops being one
paragraphs.text: How long the embryo stage lasts depends on the species. In zebrafish it ends when a bone called the cleithrum becomes visible. Animals that hatch from eggs, such as birds, are usually no longer called embryos after hatching, and in animals whose young develop inside a parent, the name ends at birth. Because species differ so much in how far they develop before hatching or birth, one textbook notes that scientists commonly read embryology broadly as the study of how animals develop.

paragraphs.heading: Plant embryos
paragraphs.text: Flowering plants make embryos too. After pollen fertilizes an ovule, their DNA combines into a single-cell zygote that develops into an embryo, which is one part of a seed. The seed also holds endosperm, a nutrient-rich tissue that helps support the young plant, and a protective seed coat. The zygote's first division is uneven, giving a small apical cell and a large basal cell, and the apical cell goes on to form most of the grown plant, including its stem, leaves and roots.
